awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Streamlining Liquid Biopsy Sample Preparation Through Automated Bisulfite Conversion
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is the development of an automated system that dramatically improves the preparation of blood-based cancer tests, known as liquid biopsies. Liquid biopsy has the potential to detect cancer earlier and for therapeutic monitoring and minimal residual disease testing by analyzing circulating tumor DNA shed by tumors into the bloodstream. However, the current preparation process is lengthy, expensive, and requires highly-skilled labor, limiting its widespread use. This project seeks to overcome these limitations by developing a miniaturized, cost-effective instrument that automates the most time-consuming and error-prone step in the workflow. By reducing labor costs, plastic waste, and sample handling errors, this innovation can make cancer screening faster, more cost-effective, and more accessible, especially for low- and mid-throughput clinics and labs. If successful, this technology will help bring non-invasive cancer testing to more patients, supporting faster diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring, better treatment decisions, and improved health outcomes, while reducing the economic burden of cancer care.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop a microfluidic-based system that automates bisulfite conversion, a critical process in preparing tumor DNA for epigenetic analysis. Traditional methods require over 40 manual steps and expose DNA to harsh conditions for extended periods, resulting in significant sample loss and variability. This project will address these limitations by creating a disposable cartridge that enables efficient chemical processing of DNA in a small-volume format, coupled with a benchtop instrument that precisely controls fluid movement and processing. The research will focus on optimizing reaction conditions to maintain high DNA recovery and conversion efficiency while reducing processing time. The anticipated outcome is a functional prototype capable of producing high-quality results comparable to gold-standard manual protocols, but with minimal human intervention. This technical advance will remove a major bottleneck in cancer diagnostics and lay the groundwork for fully automated sample preparation systems in molecular testing.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Liquid biopsy tests analyze small fragments of DNA circulating in the bloodstream and can support early cancer detection, therapeutic selection, and disease monitoring. However, isolating this cell-free DNA from blood plasma remains a major technical bottleneck. Existing methods are often labor-intensive, sensitive to operator technique, and can lose a substantial portion of the already limited cell free DNA (cfDNA) available in a patient sample. The goal of this NSF Phase I project was to determine whether cfDNA isolation could be transferred into an enclosed, automated cartridge system while increasing cfDNA recovery, process reproducibility, and compatibility with downstream molecular testing.

During Phase I, Avant Genomics designed, fabricated, and tested a single-use fluidic cartridge and a benchtop automation platform capable of performing cfDNA isolation and purification. The team evaluated multiple cartridge and instrument concepts, optimized the underlying chemistry, identified and addressed sources of DNA and particle loss, and refined the system for scalable manufacturing. Testing demonstrated that the cartridge architecture could preserve or improve performance relative to an optimized manual laboratory method. A refined cartridge subsystem recovered an average of 69.4% of the available cell-free DNA, compared with 67.3% using the optimized benchtop method. Testing of the integrated, injection-molded cartridge and instrument platform achieved an average recovery of 85.7%, compared with 68.7% for the corresponding manual control. The method demonstrated its ability to selectively capture cfDNA over interfering genomic DNA (gDNA) and preserved detectable cancer-associated mutations, supporting its suitability for downstream molecular analysis. Together, these results established the technical feasibility of performing high-recovery cfDNA isolation within an enclosed and fully automated system.

The project advanced both the scientific understanding and practical engineering of automated liquid biopsy sample preparation. In particular, the work showed that scaling these workflows does not have to come at the expense of cfDNA recovery when cartridge geometry, fluid handling, and magnetic particle capture are designed as an integrated system. The project produced an injection-molded cartridge design, a multi-sample test platform, and software-controlled workflows that provide a foundation for continued product development. The broader impact of this work is the potential to make liquid biopsy testing more consistent, efficient, and accessible across hospital and diagnostic laboratories, academic research centers, and other molecular testing environments. By reducing manual handling and preserving more of the limited, relevant genetic material present in a blood sample, this technology will ultimately help laboratories generate more reliable results while reducing workflow variability, quantity not sufficient (QNS) failures, and the volume of patient sample required.
